issues.description: The problem statement specifies that Farm should aggregate animals using a List and initialize it with an ArrayList in the no-arg constructor, but the reference solution implements the animals collection as a Queue backed by a LinkedList (Queue<Animal> animals = new LinkedList<>()). This type mismatch (List/ArrayList vs Queue/LinkedList) contradicts the specified data structure and the UML, and may confuse students about which collection type they are expected to use and what getter/setter signatures to implement.
issues.suggestedFix: Make the collection type consistent across artifacts. Either change the solution to use List<Animal> animals = new ArrayList<>() with matching getter/setter signatures to reflect the UML and problem statement, or update the problem statement and UML to accept a Queue/LinkedList implementation and explicitly allow that alternative. Preferably align the solution with the stated requirement (List/ArrayList) to avoid student confusion.

issues.description: The problem statement explicitly requires the Farm to use a List implemented as an ArrayList for the animals collection, but the solution defines the same conceptual attribute using a Queue implemented with a LinkedList. This uses different type identifiers for the same conceptual entity (collection of animals) and may confuse students about the required type and API to use.
issues.suggestedFix: Align the solution with the problem statement by declaring the animals attribute as a List<Animal> and initializing it with an ArrayList in the no-argument constructor (e.g., private List<Animal> animals; this.animals = new ArrayList<>();). Alternatively, update the problem statement to allow Queue/LinkedList if the queue semantics are intentional. Ensure method implementations use the List API or document the chosen collection type consistently.
